results.notes:
GROUP VERDICT: 3 FAIL, 4 CANNOT DETERMINE, 0 PASS. Nothing in "Neck & misc" is ready to release to manufacture.

THE HEADLINE, IN ONE LINE: all three printed neck parts have a sub-1 mm structural wall in the load path that carries the head, and the repo's own DFM sweep found only one of them.

Measured minimum walls (my own probes on Pollen's meshes, pure-Python STL ray-intervals; script at /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-leifrydenfalk/191ca988-e752-45fb-a6f7-89dde34532e7/scratchpad/stlprobe.py):
  neck             0.8500 mm  hole-to-edge ligament x4 (docs/DFM.md HAS this number but files it as a table row, not a defect)
  neck_pitch       0.8000 mm  D7.6/D6.0 centre-tube wall AND D4.4-counterbore-to-D18-disc ligament x4 (docs/DFM.md MISSES this - it reports "0.376 (sliver)" and calls it an edge chamfer)
  yaw_roll_motion  0.7500 mm  XL330 case-screw ligaments x4 (docs/DFM.md OMITS THE PART ENTIRELY - it is absent from that file's 18-part table, so no inspect.thinnest_wall run exists)
The two-perimeter floor at a 0.4 mm nozzle is 0.80 mm. yaw_roll_motion is BELOW it; the other two sit exactly on it with zero margin and no infill.

Three defects that are geometry, not judgement, and that a shop will hit on day one:
1. neck_pitch: the four D4.4 counterbores are exactly TANGENT to the D7.6 centre tube (counterbore inner edge r = 6.0 - 2.2 = 3.800; tube OD r = 3.800). Zero wall, four times, in the head-yaw load path. The mesh confirms it - at z = -15.2 the tube survives only as four islands between the counterbores.
2. yaw_roll_motion: the D4.6 x 0.5 countersinks at (7.5, +/-8) BREAK OUT through the +x plate edge (countersink reaches x 9.80 against a plate edge at 9.50, and the 1 mm rim chamfer takes the top face back to 8.50). Measured: the outboard ligament is present at z 17.0 and gone at z 17.8.
3. tire/rim: the tire's central bead (root D16.2000) sits between two D20.2000 rim flanges. Assembly demands 24.69% sustained hoop stretch over a flange, or a two-shot overmould. There is no axial slide-on. Nobody has written this down anywhere.

THE ROLLER ACCESSORY CANNOT BE RELEASED AT ALL, for two independent reasons:
- The wheel bearing does not exist. The rim's journal is D9.8000 through a 2.0000 mm web with D12.2000 x 2.8000 pockets; the blade's axle is a D2.0500/D2.7000 screw. 3.55 mm of radial slop on a wheel, and neither declared bearing (22x16x4, 15x10x3) fits either bore. Plus 2.4000 mm of unconstrained axial float (7.6000 mm rim in a 10.0000 mm slot, with the blade's bosses sitting inside the rim bore so they never touch its faces).
- The blade bolts to `ankle_l_v1`/`ankle_r_v1`, not to the shipping `ankle_left`/`ankle_right` - a 9.9981 mm difference in Y. This is critical finding #4 in its most consequential form: the roller kit's entire mounting interface is defined against a superseded ankle revision, and the roller MJCF deletes foot_left/foot_right/sole_left/sole_right completely (0 occurrences vs 9 in the walking XML) while images/CATALOG.md reads the photos as the roller mounting to a "slot on the top surface" of the FOOT. Both cannot be true.

THE DIMENSIONAL-TRUTH FILE IS STALE FOR EXACTLY THIS GROUP. out/verify/mech_dims.json marks neck, neck_pitch and yaw_roll_motion as "rebuilt": false, and docs/BOM.md and docs/PARTS.md both say "no folder". All three DO have complete ce-parts folders with T1 trust computed 2026-09-02T03:42:36 and refcheck evidence from 2026-09-01T19:3x. I verified the rebuilds independently: neck p95 0.0008 mm both ways, bbox delta 0.000, 5/5 features; neck_pitch p95 0.0071/0.0073 mm, volume ratio 1.0000, 21/21 features. Those two rebuilds are excellent and the paperwork does not say so. Fix the paperwork before a shop reads it and builds the wrong thing.

yaw_roll_motion IS THE ONE REBUILD NOT TO TRUST. p95 0.9048 mm ours->ref against a 1.00 mm limit (max 2.605 mm, within_tol 0.9762), graded against the DECIMATED 1242-tri simulator mesh, with 13 features present in our model and absent from the reference (5 holes/1 boss ref vs 16 holes/3 bosses ours). The part README argues those 13 are real vendor features the low-poly cannot resolve - that is an argument, not evidence. It is also the ONLY one of 30 slugs whose print orientation ce-slice could not solve ("auto-orient crashed the slicer with -100 on this mesh"; sliced as modelled), so its 4.7084 g / 0.2592 h figures are for an unverified orientation. Do not cut tooling from this rebuild. This is the same class of problem as critical finding #1 (the head mesh) one link down the chain.

PROCESS RECOMMENDATION THAT CHANGES A PART: microduck-neck-plate should be 2.0 mm laser-cut or stamped SHEET, not FDM PLA. It is a plain flat blank - 4 holes, R2 corners, no 3D feature at all - and images/CATALOG.md reads the product photographs as "grey folded-sheet brackets" on the neck, with press_watching.jpg showing "neck sheet bracket hole pattern". Sheet removes the 0.85 mm ligament problem outright and removes anisotropy from the part that carries the entire 279.92 g head stack. Whether the shipped part is metal is CANNOT DETERMINE - SPEC sec.6 records that the only published word on process is "four printed colourways".

PROCESS FOR THE OTHER TWO: keep FDM at every volume in evidence. docs/PRODUCTION.md sec.2.2 puts the "22 small grey brackets" on FDM even at 1,000 units ([XM1]: a 17 mm part breaks even at 2,000 units), and moulds only the 9 visible parts. Draft is therefore NOT needed on neck, neck_pitch or yaw_roll_motion. If that decision is ever reversed, PRODUCTION.md is already explicit that "a moulded version needs draft, uniform walls and side-actions for the bearing bores... a redesign, not a re-quote [PL4]".

BEARING ENGAGEMENT, TWO PARTS: neck_pitch's head-yaw boss is D16.0000 x 1.9000 long carrying a 4.0000 mm-wide 22x16x4 ring = 47.5%. yaw_roll_motion's horn-side boss is the same 1.9000 mm; its roll-side boss is D16.0000 x 4.0000 = 100%. ce-connections/press-fit-bearing-22x16x4 names this exact defect ("the 1.95 mm bosses carry the 4 mm ring at ~49%") and refuses both verdicts, and it is explicit that NO ISO 286 class can be assigned to an FDM PLA seat - "the fit verdict on those pairs is per-measurement, not per-class". So every drawing in this group must call for a reamed-and-gauged bearing seat with measured_d_mm recorded per piece, not a fit class.

NO FEA EXISTS FOR ANY PART IN THIS GROUP. out/stress/report.json covers only shin (SF 7.51 PASS), ankle (2.02 PASS), hip-bracket (6.42 PASS) and upper-leg-left (CANNOT DETERMINE, gmsh failed on overlapping facets). The neck plates are the thinnest loaded section on the robot and have never been analysed; the roller_blade takes the entire 737.2 g machine through two 2.5 mm plates and two 1.7678 mm arms with impact and edging components the 20 N walking convention does not contain, and has never been analysed. These are the two FEA runs to commission first.

PRINT REALITY FOR THE GROUP (out/print/slice.json, BambuStudio 02.08.02.61 via ce-slice, Bambu H2S, 0.4 nozzle, 0.20 mm layer, Bambu PLA Basic at 1.26 g/cm3, sliced 2026-09-02): neck-plate 0.5523 g x2 = 1.1046 g / 0.0705 h (no warning); neck-pitch-bracket 4.3782 g / 0.3291 h ("floating regions - enable supports"); yaw-roll-motion 4.7084 g / 0.2592 h ("floating regions; sliced AS MODELLED"). Group total 10.1912 g and 0.6588 h = 4.67% of the day's 218.29 g PLA and 6.63% of its 9.93 h. rim, tire, roller_blade and speaker are not in the slice set at all - their mass and cycle time are CANNOT DETERMINE.

FIVE WORK ITEMS, IN ORDER (all resolvable in-house; none is a question for Leif):
1. Widen microduck-neck-plate by 3.0 mm in y (20.0 -> 23.0) to bring the edge ligament from 0.8500 to 2.3500 mm (1.02 x d), or move it to 2.0 mm sheet. Then re-refcheck - it will no longer match Pollen's mesh, which is the correct outcome and must be recorded as a deliberate divergence.
2. Fix neck_pitch's D4.4/D7.6 tangency: drop the horn bolt circle to D11.0 or open the tube to D8.4 to recover a 0.8 mm wall on both sides.
3. Fix yaw_roll_motion's four 0.7500 mm ligaments (extend the plate 1.0 mm at each x edge) and resolve the countersink breakout. Then re-run ce-slice orientation on it - the crash is a bug to chase, not a result to accept.
4. Run inspect.thinnest_wall and the full dfm.measure sweep on yaw-roll-motion, and add rim/tire/roller_blade to docs/DFM.md - four parts in this group have never been through the repo's own DFM tool.
5. Resolve the roller wheel journal (what bearing or bush is D9.8 or D12.2) and the v1-vs-v2 ankle question from a teardown photo or a production unit. Until then the roller accessory produces no drawings.

METHOD AND ITS LIMITS: every dimension above is measured, not recalled. bboxes cross-checked against out/verify/mech_dims.json (they agree to 4 dp on all seven parts). All other geometry is my own ray-interval probing of Pollen's binary STLs at 1000x (reference metres -> mm), which reads facet intersections exactly; on a revolved mesh a radius read this way is the inscribed polygon, so radii carry a small negative bias against the true surface (D20.2000 on the rim flange is the mesh value, not a certified diameter). Every one of these meshes is a DECIMATED CC BY-SA-NC simulation asset, not CAD. SPEC sec.7 lists what that costs: no official CAD/STEP, no drawings, no tolerances, no threads. docs/PARTS.md sec.1 flag 1 says the same. Nothing in this group has ever been measured on a physical part.

dfm_issues: STRUCTURAL - THE GOVERNING ISSUE. First-order out-of-plane bending check at the repo's own 20 N design load (out/stress/report.json load_basis): section modulus of the full 36.000 mm width at 1.000 mm thick is Z = b*t^2/6 = 6.000 mm3; at the net section through the hole centreline (17.000 mm of material) Z = 2.833 mm3. A 20 N hip reaction on a 17.500 mm arm gives M = 350 N.mm -> 58.3 MPa on the gross section, 123.5 MPa on the net section, against PLA's 50 MPa class ultimate. Even the most favourable simply-supported case (span 57.000, load at x 17.500) gives M = 177.5 N.mm -> 62.7 MPa. Every reasonable support assumption lands above the allowable, i.e. SF 0.40 to 0.86. The plate CANNOT be a standalone load path; it only works as the bottom face of a box closed by power_support and the two shells, and NOTHING IN THIS REPO HAS VERIFIED THAT BOX.
Direct tension/shear in a single 1.500 mm2 ligament at 20 N is 13.3 MPa (SF 3.76 vs PLA 50 MPa class) - the ligaments survive pure tear-out; it is bending that kills the plate.

ANISOTROPY: printed flat (the sliced orientation) the plate is 5 layers at 0.2 mm. In-plane bending tension runs along the layers (favourable), but the four locating pins are loaded in interlayer shear (unfavourable) and are the first thing to snap during assembly.
The four pins are 10 layers of a cone shrinking from O1.80 to O1.59 - the slicer will round the tip; expect O1.6-1.7 at the top, not O1.59.
1.000 mm is exactly 5 layers with no infill anywhere - the part is 100 % perimeter, so wall count and flow calibration set its strength, not infill density.
NOT MOULDABLE AS DRAWN: 1.000 mm is below the Protolabs minimum wall for both PC (1.016 mm) and ABS (1.143 mm).
The 6.000 x 12.000 cable slot sits on the plate centreline and removes the exact material the bending check most needs.

dfm_issues: THE LATCH FAILS IN PLA - THIS IS THE GOVERNING DEFECT. First-order Euler-Bernoulli cantilever, all inputs measured: t = 1.181 mm, free length to the hook L = 9.183 mm (root z -12.917 to nose z -22.100), required ride-over delta = 5.128 mm (nose y 31.309 minus tongue face y 26.181). Max surface strain e = 3*t*delta/(2*L^2) = 3*1.181*5.128/(2*84.33) = 10.8 %. PLA's class elongation at break is 6 % (materials.json). If instead the user presses the tongue TIP (13.269 mm from root) to release, the tip must travel 9.27 mm to lift the hook 5.128 mm and root strain is 9.33 %. Both exceed 6 %. The deflection at which PLA reaches 6 % is 2.856 mm at the hook; PETG at 9.5 % XY reaches it at 4.523 mm - still short of the measured 5.128 mm. Only a nylon-class material clears it, or the tongue must be thinned/lengthened, or the spring must become a metal part. PLA's fatigue_mpa and fatigue_cycles are both null, so cycle life is CANNOT DETERMINE even below the strain limit - and this feature is cycled every battery change on a robot with ~1 h runtime.

ANISOTROPY OF THE LATCH: printed upright (Z-up, 83 mm tall) the layer planes are normal to the tongue's length and the bending stress pulls straight across layer bonds - guaranteed delamination. out/print/PRINT.md's chosen orientation ('tall cradle laid on its back') is the correct one and MUST be locked as a drawing note, not left to the slicer's auto-orient.

UNDERCUT - the retaining lips project 1.973 mm inward over the battery pocket in the -y direction relative to the natural +y draw. A two-plate tool cannot form them. Moulding needs a side action per rail, or the lips must be moved onto the parting line.

DRAFT is currently ~1.00 deg per side on the rails and ~1.02 deg on the ribs (both measured). Protolabs' guidance is 0.5 deg for vertical faces, 2 deg for most situations, 3 deg minimum for light texture. It will release from a polished tool; it needs a redraft to 2 deg for a production tool.

A 1.6 mm FR4 board will not fit a 0.200 mm gap, so either the bar stands off on the pins (in which case the 0.200 mm is a modelling artefact of the decimated mesh) or the real PCB is a thin flex. ANISOTROPY: printed bar-flat, the eye annulus is loaded in-plane (favourable). But the screw clamp load is applied perpendicular to the layers, so the 1.500 mm bar is in interlayer compression - acceptable - while any prying at the notch is interlayer tension.
No electrical clearance/creepage analysis exists for a plastic bar clamped over a battery-contact PCB carrying an 8.2 V pack.

This part lives in body jaw_soft, i.e. the head, and COMPARISON.html states plainly: 'Pollen's simulation head (top_head_shell, 91.751 x 122.688 x 46.339 mm) is markedly longer front-to-back than the compact domed head in every product photograph... Head tooling or prints cut from the sim mesh will not match the product.' motor_support's INTERNAL features are dimensioned by real hardware (XL330 body 20.0 x 34.0 x 26.0 per the ROBOTIS e-manual, the M12 lens and the IMX219) and are trustworthy. Its OUTLINE and its four O2.700 mounting holes are dimensioned by the head shell and are NOT. Release the internals, hold the outline and the hole pattern.

THE LENS BORE BRIDGES. In the sliced orientation ('plate flat, servo pockets up') the O17.650 tube axis is horizontal, so its top arc sags: it comes out oval and undersize. docs/DFM.md's standing rule applies - 'Horizontal bores that carry a bearing or press-fit must be reamed'. Here it is worse than a press fit: it is the camera's optical datum. Either bore/ream it after printing to O17.650 +0.10/-0.00 with a coaxiality callout, or reorient the print with the tube vertical (which then stands the 73.5 mm base plate on edge and needs supports everywhere).
1.190 mm at the first lens-tube ring is the thinnest true wall on the part - 3 perimeters at a 0.4 mm nozzle, no infill, and it is the ring nearest the lens.

THE MOUTH-SERVO ARCH IS AN UNSUPPORTED BRIDGE: a 1.600 mm shell spanning 25.400 mm (r_out 12.700) in any orientation that keeps the base plate flat. Combined with the slicer's own 'floating cantilever - enable supports' warning on the roof (z 17.500-19.200 over the east half), this part needs supports in production and the 0.20mm Standard preset does not add them.

THREE MUTUALLY PERPENDICULAR PULL DIRECTIONS (base holes z, barrel y, lens tube x). No single-draw tool can make this part. If it is ever moulded it needs two side actions or a two-part split at the barrel.

DRAFT IS ZERO ON EVERY STRAIGHT WALL. part.py's wall constants are constant-thickness pairs read off the reference - NWALL y 16.200/17.950, SWALL y -15.950/-14.200, WSTRIP x -26.460/-24.690, NE_WALL x 9.800/11.570 - i.e. 0.00 deg. The only drafted features are the crown arcs, which part.py explicitly annotates 'mid-draft' (CRS_R 7.600/9.700, CRN_R 7.350/9.950, 'drafts inward with z: inner 7.44 measured @z12'). Against Protolabs' 0.5 deg minimum for vertical faces, this part is not mouldable as drawn.

THERMAL: the head is a closed volume containing an RK3566 SBC, a TLV320AIC3104 codec and two servos, and this plate is the only structure in it. PLA at 55 degC class service temperature is the wrong material and no thermal analysis exists anywhere in the repo.

DFM REVIEW — HEAD & FACE (9 parts). Measured 2026-09-02. Roll-up: 5 FAIL, 4 CANNOT DETERMINE, 0 PASS. No part in this group may be released to tooling today.

== WHERE EVERY NUMBER COMES FROM ==
[MD] out/verify/mech_dims.json (2026-09-02, FreeCAD Mesh.BoundBox, reference metres x1000) — the bbox truth.
[FT] out/measure/face-group-features.txt + out/measure/bhs_features.txt — existing cylinder fits (cecad.meshfeatures).

Scripts: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-leifrydenfalk/191ca988-e752-45fb-a6f7-89dde34532e7/scratchpad/{feat,wall,draft,thin}.py — MOVE THESE INTO tools/ AND RE-RUN THEM INTO out/ BEFORE ANYONE QUOTES OFF THEM; they are scratchpad files today and are therefore not yet repo evidence.

[DFM] docs/DFM.md — the 2 x 0.4 = 0.80 mm two-perimeter floor; ream/drill-and-tap rules.
[PT] docs/PARTS.md; [SP] SPEC.md; [PR] images/PROPORTIONS.md; [CMP] COMPARISON.html Rev B; [PROC] docs/production/process.md (source IDs JC2, PL1, PL4, XM1, HP, LM3); [CN1] ce-connections/press-fit-bearing-15x10x3; [CN2] ce-connections/spline-xl330-horn; [SPEC-J] spec/specs-published.json; [ST] out/stress/report.json.

== TOLERANCE BASIS (there is no Pollen drawing; every tolerance below is OURS) ==
General form: ISO 2768-m. Fits quoted in ISO 286 terms; the only ISO 286 numbers I use are the ones ce-connections/press-fit-bearing-15x10x3 derives and records in its own compat.py (10 k6 = +0.001/+0.010 mm, 10 h6 = -0.009/0). Thread class 6H/6g. Moulded-part dimensional-class standards (DIN 16742 TG) were NOT read this session — CANNOT DETERMINE which TG a supplier should be held to. FDM as-printed capability is NOT sourced either: docs/PARTS.md §5 only states holes print 0.1-0.3 mm undersize; that is the only as-printed deviation figure in the repo.

== FINDING A — THE WHOLE GROUP INHERITS THE HEAD-MESH DEFECT (critical finding 1) ==
top_head_shell measures 91.7595 x 122.6900 x 46.3361 mm [MD]. COMPARISON.html Rev B §1/§5: "markedly longer front-to-back than the compact domed head in every product photograph, and the prominent eye bezel is absent from the sim mesh… Tooling cut from this mesh would give the wrong head." The one quantified check in the repo is images/PROPORTIONS.md: head-length/total-height is 0.46 in the CAD against 0.42 (cream) and 0.39 (graphite) measured off the store profile photographs — the sim head is ~10-18% too long in proportion, part of which is photographic foreshortening (PROPORTIONS.md says the head is pitched down in those shots). That is the only number; a metrology check has never been done (RELEASE.html Table 1, "Simulation/validation" row: physical laser-scan not done).
CONSEQUENCE: the defect is not confined to top_head_shell. bottom_head_shell (116.7483 long), face_part, noenoeil and jaw are all children of MJCF body jaw_soft and are dimensioned to the same head form. If the head shortens, all five change. So all five are FAIL as tooling inputs regardless of their own DFM state.

== FINDING B — THE DESIGN WALL IS 1.700 mm, NOT THE 2 mm SPEC.md §6 CLAIMS ==
Independently measured on three separate parts [NEW]: top_head_shell median 1.7100, p25 1.6956; bottom_head_shell median 1.7131, p25 1.6978; jaw p05-p25 1.6970-1.6988. Scatter across three parts is 0.021 mm. Read that as a nominal 1.700 mm wall. SPEC.md §6 ("2 mm shell walls") and docs/production/process.md ("1 mm shell walls in the meshes (SPEC §6)") are both wrong and disagree with each other; fix both to 1.700 mm. Caveat: these are Pollen's DECIMATED export, and SPEC.md §8 puts the decimation floor at p95 surface distance 1.0 mm — so 1.700 mm carries an unquantified decimation error and must be confirmed against a real part or a B-rep before it becomes a drawing dimension.

== FINDING C — FOUR SUB-0.80 mm WALLS THAT ARE NOT KNIFE-EDGES ==
docs/DFM.md's own rule is that a reading under 0.80 mm is "almost always a knife-edge". These four are not; I located each one and each sits on substantial facet area or repeats at an exact modelled value:
1. top_head_shell RIM FLANGE 0.7004-0.7331 mm over z = 0.50-1.52, on facets of 7.435, 29.919 and 50.463 mm^2 (two rear-corner rim faces at x = +/-45.24, y = -49.98 are 50.463 mm^2 each). The mating rim of the largest cosmetic part is 0.70 mm — below the 0.80 mm two-perimeter floor [DFM], and it is the FIRST layer in the sliced orientation ("dome up, rim down" [SL]) where elephant-foot widens it. FIX: thicken the rim flange to >= 1.200 mm.
2. bottom_head_shell 0.6184/0.6203 mm at (+/-42.6, -15.61, -0.38) and 0.6772/0.6804 mm at (+/-37.4, 22.0, 0.53) — small facets (0.13-0.99 mm^2), i.e. narrow strips, but repeated left/right, so modelled, not noise. FIX: >= 1.000 mm.
3. face_part 0.3000 mm EXACTLY, repeated over ~14 sampled facets spanning z 19.63-20.37 at x 11.92-12.02, y -55.20. This is the skin between the front cosmetic face (y = -55.5) and the Ø2.050 x 4.000 hole at (12.6, -53.2, 20.0) [FT], whose near end is at y = -55.2. A 0.300 mm cosmetic skin over a screw hole. The mirrored hole at (32.4, -53.2, 20.0) has the same condition; the pair straddle x = 22.5, and the ToF site sits 22.4 mm from the camera axis [SP §3], so these are most likely the ToF module's two fixings behind a blind cosmetic skin. FDM will drop or single-extrude 0.300 mm; injection will short-fill or sink it. FIX: either break through (accept a visible port) or thicken to >= 0.800 mm FDM / >= 1.000 mm MJF.
4. soft_mouth_top 0.8069 mm over the part's LARGE faces — facets of 692.776, 861.254, 674.893 and 343.089 mm^2 all read 0.8069. The upper lip is a 0.807 mm TPU membrane, not a 1.9 mm lip; the 1.9 mm median comes from its edge beads. 0.807 mm is exactly the two-perimeter floor and below JLC3DP's MJF/SLS "1 mm / > 1.0 mm" minimum [PROC JC2], so it cannot be MJF'd at all, and at flow-length/wall = 87.822/0.807 = 108.8:1 in a high-viscosity TPU it is a short-shot candidate for injection.

== FINDING D — THE HEAD-CLOSE SCREW JOINT DOES NOT WORK WITH THE FASTENERS IN THE BOM ==
Measured stack [FT + NEW]: bottom_head_shell has 3 x Ø2.695 clearance holes with Ø5.500 x 2.824 counterbores below and Ø6.902 x 3.145 bosses above, at (0, +49.5), (+39.0, -49.5), (-39.0, -49.5); top_head_shell has the matching 3 x Ø2.100 x 11.200 blind posts at the same XY, with Ø2.800 x 0.800 lead-ins. Ø2.100 = the M2.5 thread-forming size (2.5 - 0.45 pitch = 2.05, +0.05). So the head closes with 3 x M2.5 driven up from below into printed posts.
(i) GRIP LENGTH before any thread = 2.824 + 2.004 + 3.145 = 7.973 mm. docs/PARTS.md §5's community purchase estimate lists only "M2.5x6 x20" — an M2.5x6 cannot even reach the dome. Minimum useful is M2.5x12 (4.0 mm engagement); M2.5x16 gives 8.0 mm of the 11.2 mm available. Screw length is CANNOT DETERMINE (no Pollen BOM); the geometry sets the floor at 12 mm.
(ii) CLEARANCE 2.695 - 2.500 = 0.195 mm diametral = 0.0975 mm radial float per hole, across a bolt pattern spanning 78.0 mm (rear pair) and 99.0 mm (rear to front). True position on all six mating features must hold Ø0.195 MMC over a 122.7 mm part or the head will not close. That is tighter than ISO 2768-m and tighter than any FDM process in this repo. FIX: open the bottom-shell holes to Ø2.900 (ISO 273 medium for M2.5) and let the counterbore carry the head.
(iii) THREE screws on a 91.76 x 122.69 mm rim, with that rim measured at 0.70 mm (Finding C1): the seam will gap between fixings on the most visible part of the product.
(iv) ANISOTROPY: sliced dome-up/rim-down [SL], the layer planes are perpendicular to the post axis, so the M2.5 thread is formed straight across layer boundaries and pull-out is carried by inter-layer bond. Use M2.5 heat-set inserts, as SPEC.md §6 already prescribes for loaded threads.

== FINDING E — MOULDABILITY, MEASURED (none of these parts is mould-ready) ==
Undercut = % of surface area shadowed along the pull it faces. Draft = % of near-parallel wall area under the stated angle. Pull axis is the mesh's own frame.
  top_head_shell   pull Z: 4.43% undercut; 47.05% of area is wall-like; of those walls 9.72% < 0.5 deg, 20.73% < 3 deg.
  bottom_head_shell pull Z: 9.75% undercut; 54.25% wall-like; 24.18% < 0.5 deg, 79.06% < 3 deg  <- effectively draftless.
  face_part        pull Y: 13.34% undercut; 26.52% wall-like; 91.51% < 0.5 deg  <- zero draft.
  jaw              pull Z: 6.29% undercut / pull X: 53.25% undercut  -> MOULD ON Z, trunnions become 2 side actions (PL4: GBP 1,000-2,000 per cam).
  noenoeil         pull Y: 24.09% undercut; 100.00% of walls < 0.5 deg  <- perfect zero-draft cylinders.
  m12_lens_holder  pull Y: 50.65% undercut; 94.60% < 0.5 deg.
  jaw_soft (TPU)   pull Z: 5.64% undercut; 51.93% < 0.5 deg  (elastomer strips modest undercuts — the least bad).
  soft_mouth_top   pull Z: 3.51% undercut; 29.09% < 0.5 deg  (flattest, most mould-friendly form in the group).
This is the measured proof of docs/production/process.md §5.1's assertion that a moulded version is "a redesign, not a re-quote". Flow-length/wall ratios for a tool designer: top_head_shell 72.2:1, bottom_head_shell 68.7:1, jaw 53.9:1, face_part 48.4:1, jaw_soft 44.5:1, soft_mouth_top 108.8:1. Moulding resin is CANNOT DETERMINE for every part — Pollen's only process word is "printed" [PROC PK] — and until a resin is chosen, shrink is unknown and no steel can be sized.

== FINDING F — THE MOUTH JOINT, MEASURED END TO END ==
jaw hinge axis is X at z = 7.5 in the jaw's frame [NEW]. Left side: a Ø10.000 x 2.700 boss at x = -38.35 with a Ø12.000 x 0.300 shoulder and a Ø2.000 x 7.003 axial hole — the inner-ring seat of the 15x10x3 bearing [CN1]. Engagement 2.700/3.000 = 90.0% of the ring width; ce-connections/press-fit-bearing-15x10x3 records the same deliberate proud-ring pattern on the ankle (2.3 mm pocket for a 3 mm ring). Right side: Ø6.000 x 4.137 hub bore + 4 x Ø2.200 on a Ø12.000 PCD at (0,+/-6) and (+/-6,0) about (y 0, z 7.5), inside Ø16.000 x 2.767 register bosses on BOTH faces — that is exactly the XL330 horn interface ce-connections/spline-xl330-horn measures (Ø16.0 x 3.0 disc, 4 x Ø1.6 tapped on a Ø12.0 circle). So the jaw is driven by ID 34 on the right and idles on a bearing on the left.
LOAD: press states ~100 g beak lift [SPEC-J beak_lift_capacity, The Register 2026-08-27]. Worst case at the extreme beak tip, y = -59.7105 from the hinge: 0.100 x 9.80665 x 0.0597105 = 0.05856 N.m. XL330-M288 stall is 0.52 N.m at 5 V / 0.60 N.m at 6 V [SPEC-J, ROBOTIS eManual] -> the SERVO has 8.88x / 10.25x margin. The PART's margin is unknown: out/stress/report.json covers only shin (SF 7.51), ankle (SF 2.02), hip-bracket (SF 6.42) and upper-leg (CANNOT DETERMINE, gmsh failed on overlapping facets). No head or beak part has ever been analysed. The jaw trunnion root is the obvious next FEA case.

results.summary:
MICRODUCK — PROCESS SELECTION, ECONOMICS AND PRINT PROFILES (2026-09-02)

=== 0. THE HEADLINE, AND IT IS NOT THE ONE THE BRIEF EXPECTED ===

Injection moulding does NOT pay for any part of this robot at any quantity up to 10,000, measured against the five FDM printers this workshop already owns (ce-cad/cecad/data/printers.json: 2x H2D, 1x X2D, 2x H2S). The cheapest break-even in the whole set is the top-head-shell at N* = 5,401 units; 20 of the 30 printed slugs have NO break-even at all below 10,000 (moulded piece price exceeds in-house FDM unit cost outright, so N* is undefined — reported as null, never as a large number).

The reason is arithmetic, not opinion. In-house FDM marginal cost is $21.86–23.73 per robot for all 36 pieces (real slicer grams from out/print/slice.json, real filament prices, real machine depreciation). A moulded piece price derived from sourced inputs is $0.038–0.918 per part. The gap per part is $0.06–$1.84 — and a single aluminium Class-105 tool is $1,500–8,000 (Jaycon 2026). $1,500 / $1.84 = 815 at best; but the parts with the biggest gap are also the ones needing the biggest tools ($5,000–8,000), which is why the real numbers land at 5,401–48,811.

THE DECISION FLIPS ENTIRELY IF YOU DO NOT OWN THE PRINTERS. At a bought farm hour of $4/h (LM2/PR2/GC), unit cost per robot rises to $62.06 and break-even collapses: top-head-shell 974, bottom-head-shell 1,169, soles 1,144/1,148, foot L/R 1,527/1,529, ankle L/R 1,539/1,545, jaw-soft 1,736, power-support 1,790, neck-pitch-bracket 1,928, motor-support 2,008. So the correct statement is: **the process decision is a decision about who owns the machine hour, not about the part.** Owning printers is worth $79,322 of H2S capex (64 machines) against $94,500–195,000 of tooling for the same 30 parts — and the printers are re-taskable, the tools are not.

=== 1. WHAT ACTUALLY BINDS AT 1,000 AND 10,000: TIME, NOT MONEY ===

12.346 h of per-piece print time per robot (out/print/slice.json, sum of seconds_total; PRINT.md states a plate prints faster than the sum of its parts, so this is an UPPER BOUND — the plate time is not in the repo and is CANNOT DETERMINE).

5 printers x 24 h x 0.90 uptime (PR2 reports 90–95 % success) = 108.0 printer-h/day = 8.75 robots/day.
   1 robot      12.3 h        0.1 day
   10 robots    123.5 h       1.1 days
   100 robots   1,234.6 h     11.4 days
   1,000 robots 12,346 h      114.3 days
   10,000       123,460 h     1,143 days = 3.13 YEARS on the current fleet.

To build 10,000 in 90 days needs 63.5 H2S = $79,322 at the $1,249 launch price (3dprint.com). That is the real capital question, and it is CHEAPER than tooling all 30 parts ($94,500–195,000) and comparable to tooling the visible 10 ($39,000–70,000). Moulding buys ~16–21 s cycles instead of 12.3 h; that throughput, not unit cost, is the only argument for a tool at 10,000.

=== 2. FOUR REASONS NO SHELL TOOL MAY BE CUT TODAY REGARDLESS OF ECONOMICS ===

(a) HEAD MESH IS WRONG. top_head_shell measures 91.7595 x 122.6900 x 46.3361 mm (out/verify/mech_dims.json, 16,120 tris) and COMPARISON.html states it "is markedly longer front-to-back than the compact domed head in every product photograph… Head tooling or prints cut from the sim mesh will not match the product." VERDICT FAIL for tooling at every quantity. Print it only as an engineering mule.
(b) LICENCE. ce-parts/microduck-trunk-shell-left|-right/component.json: origin "vendor", licence "CC BY-SA-NC 4.0 (pollen-robotics/microduck_rl README)", "usable to assemble, render, simulate and print; NOT licensed for sale (NC)". Own verdict CANNOT DETERMINE. Tooling a shell for sale is a licence breach, not a cost question. 22 of the 30 sliced STLs are vendor meshes (out/print/PRINT.md).
(c) NO PARAMETRIC REBUILD. left_shell / right_shell have rebuilt:false in mech_dims.json. Per docs/MANUFACTURING-REQUIREMENTS.md §A.3, "a vendor mesh part gets no drawing (it has no manufacturable dimensions)". A tool needs a drawing; a decimated STL is not one.
(d) A-SURFACE NEVER PHOTO-MATCHED. SPEC.md §8 sets a photo-match acceptance criterion; out/photomatch/ holds only renders and evidence/ is empty. The trunk's outer form is in exactly the unexamined position the head was in before it was examined.

=== 3. TRUNK-GROUP DFM FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE PROCESS CHOICE ===

FINDING A (trunk_base is 1.000 mm, not 3.000 mm). Direct probe: at (x -28.000, y 0.000) material along z runs 16.500–17.500 = 1.0000 mm; at a pin at (x -25.500, y -9.500) it runs 16.500–19.500 = 3.0000 mm. mech_dims.json's 3.0000 is the BOUNDING BOX over four 2.000 mm locating pins. CONSEQUENCE: a 1.000 mm nominal wall is BELOW Protolabs' moulding minimum for PC (0.040 in = 1.0160 mm) and well below ABS (0.045 in = 1.1430 mm). trunk_base is NOT an injection-moulding candidate as drawn at any quantity. It is a sheet part that happens to have been printed — recommend 1.000 mm laser-cut Al 5052-H32 or 1.000 mm G10/FR4 (materials.json FR4 in-plane 355 MPa, grade tier) with 4 pressed dowels replacing the moulded pins. Correct docs/PARTS.md row 1 and SPEC.md §4.1 to "1.000 mm plate, 3.000 mm bbox over the pins".

=== 4. THE FEA IS ONLY VALID ON A SOLID PART ===

out/stress/report.json solves solids. The 0.20mm Standard @BBL H2S preset does not print solids. A 15 %-infill bracket is not the bracket that returned SF 2.0210. CONSEQUENCE: every load-path part must be printed at 100 % infill (they are 0.55–13.35 g; the whole load-path set goes from 107.89 g as-sliced to 127.58 g solid PETG — 19.7 g for validity), or the FEA must be re-run at the printed density. There is no third option that leaves a PASS standing.

Also: out/stress/report.json covers only shin, upper-leg-left (CANNOT DETERMINE — gmsh "Invalid boundary mesh (overlapping facets) on surface 350"), ankle-left and hip-bracket. trunk_base, power_support, motor_support and BOTH SHELLS have never been solved, and Finding C has just made the shells load-bearing. sim/stress_matrix.py is written to do it (20 N standing / 60 N landing / 15 N lateral, PLA/PETG/ABS/NYLON/ASA sweep) but out/stress/ holds no matrix result.

=== 5. NO BRIM — AND docs/DFM.md CONTRADICTS THE HOUSE RULE FIVE TIMES ===

This workshop uses NO BRIM. docs/DFM.md lines 78, 89, 109, 115 and 155 call for one (power-support, shin, upper-legs, rigidity-plate, neck-plate). Those five notes must be struck. The brim-free plan, per part:
- power-support (83.4898 mm tall, 5:1 aspect): already solved by orientation — ce-slice laid it on its back ("tall cradle laid on its back to cut supports"). No brim needed.
- shin (58.0000 mm): already sliced "8 mm plate flat, rim walls up". No brim needed.
- upper-leg L/R (60.9966 mm tall, sliced servo-cavity-up): the only genuine adhesion risk. Add four modelled sacrificial mouse-ear discs (O8.000 x 0.200 mm) at the footprint corners as a separate STL, snapped off after printing. Do NOT enable a slicer brim.
- rigidity-plate (1.0000 mm) and neck-plate (2.0000 mm): the risk is WARP, not adhesion. The H2S has a 65 degC heated chamber (3dprintingindustry H2S launch specs), which is the correct mitigation. Lay flat, no brim.

=== 8. TOLERANCE BASIS ===
ISO 2768-1 Table 1 / ISO 2768-2 classes H/K/L as carried in ce-cad/cecad/machining.py, which sets ISO2768_VERIFIED = False ("TRANSCRIBED 2026-09-01 from dekmake.com/guide-to-iso-2768 and corroborated against AmesWeb and EngineersEdge… ISO 2768-1:1989 is paywalled"). Bands: 0.5–3 mm f +/-0.05 m +/-0.10; 3–6 f +/-0.05 m +/-0.10; 6–30 f +/-0.10 m +/-0.20 c +/-0.50; 30–120 f +/-0.15 m +/-0.30 c +/-0.80. ISO 2768-2 class K flatness 0.20 mm over 100 mm. Every class is a REQUIREMENT PLACED ON THE SUPPLIER. Nothing in this repo has a measured flatness, perpendicularity or printed fit, so NO PASS may be written against any geometric tolerance today.

=== 9. FASTENER SYSTEM ===
An M2 system throughout (SPEC.md §4 hole census, community-derived): O2.2 clearance x77, O4.4 counterbore x28, O1.6 tap x20, O2.4 loose x22, O2.0 tight x12, O2.7/2.8 x20, O4.8 x10. ISO 261 coarse pitch 0.400 mm; derived d2 1.740192, d3 1.509252, D1 1.566987, As 2.0732 mm2. Tightening torque and pull-out both null. WORK ITEM: measure M2 form-tap pull-out in printed PETG at a O1.600 pilot before releasing any self-tapped boss.

=== 10. CYCLE TIME, DERIVED AND ANCHORED ===
Cooling law calibrated on zetarmold's own two data points: "a 2mm wall part cooling for 10 seconds" and "A part with 4mm walls cooling for 40 seconds" — a 4x rise for 2x thickness, i.e. t_cool = 2.5 * s^2 (s in mm, t in s), which reproduces both exactly and matches RJG's statement that thickness enters squared. Cooling is 60–80 % of cycle (Jaycon 2026). Cycles derived on the FOUR trunk parts with a measured wall:
  trunk_base   s = 1.000 mm -> t_cool 2.50 s -> cycle 3.1–4.2 s (below any practical mould open/close; and the wall is under the PC moulding minimum anyway)
  banana-locker s = 1.450    -> t_cool 5.26 s -> cycle 6.6–8.8 s
  motor-support s = 1.750    -> t_cool 7.66 s -> cycle 9.6–12.8 s
  power-support s = 1.950    -> t_cool 9.51 s -> cycle 11.9–15.8 s
  trunk shells  s = 2.250    -> t_cool 12.66 s -> cycle 15.8–21.1 s
Every other part has NO measured nominal wall (docs/DFM.md reports thinnest wall, which is a knife-edge on most rows, not a nominal) -> cycle CANNOT DETERMINE, and Jaycon 2026's real reference "25 to 35 second cycle" (four-cavity) is used as the anchor instead. Sanity check on the RJG worked example: 3.3 mm tensile bar, 18.00 s simulated / 16.73 s actual cooling; the 2.5*s^2 law predicts 27.2 s — so the law RUNS CONSERVATIVE (over-predicts) against RJG by ~50 %, meaning the moulded piece prices below are if anything HIGH and the case against moulding is stronger, not weaker.

=== 11. SLA IS OUT, AND WHY ===
No resin machine exists on the roster (printers.json lists five FDM machines only) — SLA means new capex. More decisively, Protolabs Network states SLA parts "are brittle, less stable than other 3D-printed materials over long periods and inclined to experience some creep" and "generally not suitable for producing functional parts that can withstand… loads", and photopolymers "become brittle and yellow under the influence of UV light" with "aging and a change in properties… after a couple of months". A 737 g bipedal robot whose every bracket is under permanent static load, sold in four pastel colourways that sit in daylight, is the exact case those sources exclude. SLA VERDICT: FAIL for every load-path part; not selected for the cosmetic parts either, because the same UV-yellowing sentence applies to a Cream shell. The one legitimate SLA use here is a rapid A-surface appearance model of the (corrected) head before tooling — a one-off, not a process.

LOWEST safety factor in the whole robot: SF 2.0210 at 20 N (bearing_seat fixed, horn_face loaded) - and on a class-tier PLA allowable, so it is not a PASS. Re-solve on PETG at the 60 N landing case in sim/stress_matrix.py before release. O15 and O14 bores bridge on X - REAM.

decisions.part: microduck-trunk-base (trunk_base, 57.0000 x 36.0000 x 3.0000 mm BBOX over 2.000 mm pins; 1.0000 mm STRUCTURAL PLATE, 1.42 cm3)
decisions.process_by_qty: 1: FDM PETG | 10: FDM PETG | 100: FDM PETG or laser-cut sheet | 1000: LASER-CUT 1.000 mm SHEET | 10000: LASER-CUT / STAMPED SHEET. Injection moulding is REFUSED at every quantity.
decisions.unit_cost_usd: 1-10000: $0.161 flat as FDM PETG. Farm $4/h: $0.395. Moulded $0.038-$0.099 at a DERIVED 3.1-4.2 s cycle. Sheet-metal price: CANNOT DETERMINE (no laser-cutting quote in any source read).
decisions.rationale: THE ROOT BODY OF THE ENTIRE MJCF TREE (199.224 g body mass). Both hip-yaw XL330s hang under it through two O19.000 holes at (+/-17.500, -2.000) on a 35.000 mm pitch; it carries the two 22x16x4 hip-yaw idler bearings at body (6, +/-17.5, -5); power_support's two 1.940 mm flanges bolt up to it; the neck-pitch axis is dimensioned from it. Every leg load passes through this plate. FINDING A resolves the 1 mm / 3 mm conflict: the plate is 1.0000 mm (probed at (x -28.000, y 0.000): material 16.500-17.500), the 3.0000 mm is the bbox over four 2.000 mm pins (probed at (x -25.500, y -9.500): 16.500-19.500). INJECTION MOULDING IS REFUSED: 1.0000 mm is below Protolabs' minimum wall for PC (0.040 in = 1.0160 mm) and far below ABS (0.045 in = 1.1430 mm). N* 48,811 is academic. It is a flat plate with six through-holes and one slot - a SHEET PART that happens to have been printed. Going to 1.000 mm laser-cut Al 5052-H32 or 1.000 mm G10/FR4 removes the ligament risk entirely at the cost of making the four locating pins separate pressed dowels. It has NEVER been stress-solved and must be solved as an ASSEMBLY (trunk_base + power_support + left_shell + right_shell), not as a bare plate.

decisions.rationale: MOULDING REFUSED for the same reason as trunk_base: a 1.0000 mm nominal wall is under the PC (1.0160 mm) and ABS (1.1430 mm) minimums. NEVER breaks even; the moulded piece price is several times the printed one. docs/PARTS.md row 11 already flags 'or sheet - CANNOT DETERMINE; 1 mm is thin for FDM' - at 1,000+ units, laser-cut sheet is the right answer for the same reason as the chassis plate. MUST be printed dead flat (1 mm = 5 layers at 0.20 mm); printing it on edge would be 291 layers of a 1 mm wall and would fail.

Two of these span the 50.000 mm neck (neck_pitch axis at world (26.0, 14.5, 152.4), head_pitch at (26.0, 14.5, 202.4)) with an XL330 at each end, so they are load-path despite being 2 mm plates - PETG, not PLA. decisions.part: microduck-banana-pcb-locker (banana_pcb_locker, 54.0501 x 3.8000 x 6.6524 mm, 0.46 cm3, wall 1.450 mm modal bar / 0.950 eye annulus, p1 0.9204)
decisions.process_by_qty: 1-10000: FDM PETG at every quantity. Moulding REFUSED.
decisions.unit_cost_usd: 1-10000: $0.072 flat. Farm $4/h: $0.191. Moulded $0.074-$0.197 at a DERIVED 6.6-8.8 s cycle - i.e. AT OR ABOVE the printed cost.
decisions.rationale: NEVER breaks even: even at the most favourable moulded piece price ($0.074) the gap to the printed cost ($0.072) is negative. Prints in 2m20s for 0.6794 g with no warnings. BLOCKED ON A DIFFERENT AXIS ENTIRELY: the clamp stack is a nominal 0.200 mm gap (bar inner face at mesh y 35.000, power_support pin tops at y 34.800), and what fills that gap is the 'banana' battery-contact PCB - one of the three custom boards with NO published design files. The clamp CANNOT BE DIMENSIONED until that board's thickness and outline exist. Design the PCB first.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. Prefer 1.000 mm laser-cut Al 5052-H32 sheet at qty >=1000.
print_profiles.orientation: Flat, largest 57.0000 x 36.0000 face on the bed, all six holes (O2.3 x4, O19.000 x2) vertical. WHY: the plate is loaded in BENDING by both hip-yaw servos hanging under it, so the peak stress is in-plane sigma_x - printed flat that stress runs along the layer (PETG XY 51 +/- 1 MPa) and never across it (Z 35 +/- 6 MPa). Printed on edge the same bending would pull layer interfaces apart. Flat also makes all six bores vertical, so none bridges and none comes out oval.
print_profiles.supports: None. No overhangs, no slicer warning, and the four 2.000 mm locating pins print as short vertical studs.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. Mandatory: this part holds a battery under permanent static load and materials.json states PLA creeps at room temperature.
print_profiles.orientation: Laid on its back (ce-slice auto-orient: 'tall cradle laid on its back to cut supports'), NOT standing on the 83.4898 mm axis. WHY, twice over: (1) it kills the 5:1 slender aspect that docs/DFM.md wanted a brim for, and this workshop uses no brim; (2) the sprung latch tongue's bending plane must lie IN the layer plane, so the tongue flexes along fibres instead of peeling layer from layer - it is a cycled cantilever and delamination is its documented failure mode.
print_profiles.supports: YES - slicer flags 'floating regions'. Tree supports on the battery-pocket overhangs and the two 1.940 mm flanges. The quoted 13.1477 g / 38m21s EXCLUDES support material and is a lower bound.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA because Finding C makes this a load path, not a show part.
print_profiles.orientation: Flat rim (the mating face) down, dome up. WHY: the neck-pitch reaction enters through the boss cluster at mesh (16.250, -22.000, 50.000) and is reacted at the rim, so the load runs along the shell surface - rim-down puts that path in-plane. It also puts the four O5.008-5.035 bosses on the inside as upward features that build off solid material rather than as unsupported ceilings, and gives the largest flat contact patch on the bed (needed with no brim).
print_profiles.supports: None needed as sliced (no warning). Keep it that way - a support scar on the A-surface is unrecoverable. 5 walls x 0.42 mm = 2.10 mm of the 2.250 mm measured wall, so the section is effectively solid perimeter.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA, same reason.
print_profiles.orientation: Flat rim down, dome up - mirror of the left. WHY: identical load path (its boss cluster places at world (26.0, -16.75, 152.50)). It also carries the sole O1.600 x 4.700 shell-to-shell self-tap at mesh (-2.650, 42.000, 52.500); rim-down makes that pilot hole VERTICAL, which is the only orientation that gives a round, on-size pilot for a thread the whole body relies on.
print_profiles.supports: None (no slicer warning). Protect the A-surface.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Plate flat, servo pockets up. WHY: it is a 73.5000 x 54.2000 plate only 18.8000 mm deep carrying two XL330s and the electronics; flat puts the plate's bending stress in-plane and the servo pockets become upward-opening cavities instead of ceilings.
print_profiles.supports: YES - slicer flags 'floating cantilever'. Support only the cantilevered ear; 9.1993 g / 21m04s excludes it.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Bar flat on its 54.0501 mm face, eyes up. WHY: the bar clamps a PCB, so it is loaded in bending across its length; flat puts that in-plane. Eyes up makes the two O2.17 M2 holes vertical instead of bridged.
print_profiles.supports: None. NOTE the 0.16 mm layer (not 0.20): the eye annulus is only 0.950 mm modal wall with a p1 of 0.9204 mm, so it is barely two perimeters - a finer layer buys resolution on the one feature that has no margin. This invalidates the quoted 140.45 s; re-slice.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. FEA SF 7.5106 must be re-solved on PETG to become a real PASS.
print_profiles.orientation: 8.0000 mm plate flat on the bed, rim walls up. WHY: the shin carries the standing load from knee to ankle along its 58.0000 mm length. Flat puts that tension/bending along the layer (51 MPa) rather than across it (35 MPa) - printed upright, the whole 58 mm load path would be layer-adhesion-limited. Flat also removes the tall-thin-blade adhesion problem docs/DFM.md wanted a brim for.
print_profiles.supports: None as oriented. The 15 holes that ran horizontal in the upright orientation become vertical here; ream the knee and ankle pivots regardless.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Servo cavity opening up (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY THIS IS ONLY PROVISIONAL: it puts the 60.9966 mm dimension along Z, so any tension along the thigh crosses layers at 35 +/- 6 MPa. Normally that would be wrong - but out/stress/report.json returns CANNOT DETERMINE for this part (gmsh: invalid boundary mesh, overlapping facets on surface 350), so there is NO stress field to orient against. Fix the mesh, solve it, then re-decide. Cavity-up is retained meanwhile because it is the only orientation that does not need supports inside the servo pocket.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating cantilever'. NO BRIM: at 60.9966 mm tall this is the one genuine adhesion risk in the set, so add four modelled sacrificial mouse-ear discs (O8.000 x 0.200 mm) at the footprint corners as a separate STL and snap them off. Do not enable a slicer brim.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Servo cavity opening up - mirror of the left, and provisional for the same reason (no valid FEA on either thigh). 2x O5.37 hip-pivot bores run on X and bridge: REAM after printing.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating cantilever'. Mouse-ear discs, NO BRIM.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. At qty >=1000 consider 1.000 mm laser-cut sheet instead.
print_profiles.orientation: 1.0000 mm plate DEAD FLAT on the bed (5 layers at 0.20 mm). WHY: it is a stiffener spanning hip-pitch to knee, loaded in-plane; flat aligns that with the strong direction AND is the only printable orientation - on edge it would be 291 layers of a 1 mm wall and would fail outright (docs/DFM.md).
print_profiles.supports: None. NO BRIM: the risk here is warp, not adhesion, and the H2S 65 degC heated chamber is the correct mitigation. The O19 and 4x O2.2 pass straight through the 1 mm thickness and print clean when flat.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. FEA SF 6.4240 must be re-solved on PETG.
print_profiles.orientation: Bracket web down, bearing seat vertical (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY: the load runs roll_boss -> pitch_boss through the web, and web-down keeps that in-plane; bearing-seat-vertical is what stops the 22x16x4 seat printing oval. This is the densest part in the robot (22 holes in 32.4501 x 34.5000 x 19.0000) so bore roundness matters more here than anywhere else.
print_profiles.supports: None (no slicer warning). 0.16 mm layer because the minimum wall is 0.80 mm = exactly two perimeters with zero margin, and because 22 bores in this volume need the resolution. Re-slice - this invalidates the quoted 1066.91 s.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Servo pocket up, bearing bore vertical (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY: pocket-up avoids supports inside the XL330 seat; bore-vertical keeps the hip-roll bearing seat round. The part is a short link (23.0000 x 25.8000 x 20.5000) so no dimension is long enough for layer anisotropy to dominate.
print_profiles.supports: None (no warning). 8 horizontal holes O2.05-5.5 still bridge at their tops - drill and form-tap the small ones.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: 3.0000 mm plate flat, bore vertical. WHY: an idler plate is loaded in-plane by the bearing; flat aligns that with the strong direction and makes the O19 bore vertical instead of bridged. The bore is the whole function of the part - a bridged O19 comes out oval and undersize at the top.
print_profiles.supports: None. REAM the O19 if it seats a bearing.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. SF 2.0210 is the lowest in the robot and is NOT a PASS on a class-tier PLA allowable; re-solve on PETG at the 60 N landing case.
print_profiles.orientation: Bearing bore vertical (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY: the O15 and O14 bores seat a 15x10x3 bearing and a press fit; vertical is the only orientation that gives a round on-size bore without bridging. This is bought at the cost of putting part of the bearing_seat -> horn_face load path across layers - acceptable ONLY because the bore fit is a hard functional requirement and the load path is short. Re-examine once the PETG FEA exists.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. 0.16 mm layer for bore roundness on the lowest-safety-factor part in the robot. REAM O15 and O14 after printing. Confirm you are printing ankle_left (Y 36.5000) and NOT the roller-variant ankle_l_v1 (Y 46.4981).

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Bearing bore vertical - mirror of the left, same reasoning and the same trade of load-path alignment for bore roundness.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. REAM O15/O14. Confirm ankle_right (Y 36.5000), not ankle_r_v1 (Y 46.4973).

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Sole face down, toes up. WHY: the sole face is the largest flat area and the ground-reaction load enters normal to it, so sole-down puts that load into layer COMPRESSION (which layer adhesion handles fine) rather than tension. It also makes the single O1.600 blind tapped hole vertical.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. The 0.015 mm wall reading at z = -16.7 is the bottom sole chamfer, a cosmetic knife-edge, not a structural wall - ignore it. Drill and form-tap the O1.600 x 5.5 blind hole after printing.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Sole face down, toes up - mirror, same reasoning.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. Drill/tap the blind O1.600.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA. These 2 mm plates carry the whole head between two XL330s 50.000 mm apart; they are load path, not trim.
print_profiles.orientation: 2.0000 mm plate flat on the bed. WHY: the plate is a tension/compression link between the neck-pitch and head-pitch servos, loaded along its 20.0000 mm length - flat puts that in-plane. On edge, a 2 mm wall standing 20 mm tall would be entirely layer-adhesion-limited on the link that holds the head up.
print_profiles.supports: None. NO BRIM - warp is the risk, and the H2S heated chamber handles it. The 4x O2.3 that bridged in the upright orientation are vertical here.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Bearing seat vertical (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY: it holds the 22x16x4 head-yaw bearing at body (0, 20.8, -14.5); a bridged bearing seat is oval and the head yaw would bind. Bore roundness governs.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. 0.16 mm for the bearing seat. 10 horizontal holes O2.2/O6.0 still bridge; ream the O6.0, drill/tap the O2.2.

print_profiles.material: PETG (Bambu PETG Basic) - CHANGED from PLA.
print_profiles.orientation: Both bearing bores vertical. WHY: it carries TWO 22x16x4 bearings at body x = -16 and +18 straddling the head-roll axis, and both must be round and coaxial or the head roll binds. CAUTION: ce-slice recorded 'sliced AS MODELLED - auto-orient (-100) crashed the slicer on this mesh', so this orientation was NOT verified by the auto-orienter. Verify it on a real plate before production.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. REAM both O22 seats and check coaxiality; a printed pair of bores 34 mm apart is the tightest alignment requirement in the head.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - cosmetic, no sustained structural load. NOT a load path, so the PETG rule does not apply.
print_profiles.orientation: Face plate back-side down, eyes up. WHY: the visible face must never touch the bed or a support - bed texture and support scars both land on the A-surface. Back-down puts every witness mark on the hidden side, and the camera aperture (world (81.4, 0, 251.1)) and ToF window (81.4, 22.4, 249.1) print as clean vertical openings.
print_profiles.supports: None (no slicer warning). 0.12 mm layer: this is the most-looked-at surface on the robot and layer lines are the whole visual difference between a print and a moulding. This invalidates the quoted 909.99 s - re-slice.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - cosmetic.
print_profiles.orientation: Ring flat on the bed. WHY: a 30.0000 x 30.0000 ring only 9.5000 mm deep - flat is the largest contact patch, needs no support, and puts the layer lines concentric with the ring so they read as a deliberate texture rather than a defect.
print_profiles.supports: None. 0.12 mm for the same visual reason as face-part.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - trim colour. Reassess if the mouth DoF (-5 deg closed to +30 deg open, ~100 g lift) turns out to load it in sustained bending.
print_profiles.orientation: Beak underside down (ce-slice auto-orient). WHY: the upper beak surface is the A-surface and must not carry bed texture; underside-down hides every witness mark inside the mouth.
print_profiles.supports: None as sliced. Keep it that way - support scars inside a 91.4158 mm beak are hard to remove and the part is trim-coloured, so any blemish shows.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - MULE ONLY. Do not treat as a production profile: COMPARISON.html says this mesh does not match the product's head.
print_profiles.orientation: Dome up, rim down (auto-orient confirms). WHY: rim-down gives the largest flat contact patch (needed with no brim), keeps the dome's A-surface off the bed, and means supports land only inside.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating regions'. 34.6097 g / 68m46s is the largest single print in the set and EXCLUDES support material. Do not tune this profile further until the head geometry is corrected against the press photographs - you would be optimising the wrong shape.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - MULE ONLY, same block as the dome it mates to.
print_profiles.orientation: Outer face down per auto-orient. RE-EXAMINE: outer-face-down puts the visible trim-yellow surface against the bed, which is normally wrong for an A-surface. It is retained only because the part is a mule; for a production part, flip it and support the inside.
print_profiles.supports: YES - 'floating cantilever'. 28.2837 g / 59m16s excludes support.

print_profiles.material: PLA (Bambu PLA Basic) - if printed at all; make/buy is CANNOT DETERMINE and a stock M12 holder is likely cheaper.
print_profiles.orientation: Threaded bore vertical. WHY: an M12x0.5 lens thread is the entire function of the part and a bridged bore will not accept a lens. Vertical is the only orientation that gives a round thread form.
print_profiles.supports: None. 0.12 mm because a printed M12x0.5 thread at 0.20 mm layer has 2.5 layers per pitch and will not engage. Better still: buy the part.

print_profiles.material: TPU. Bambu TPU 85A is what the H2S 0.4 preset resolved to; the product durometer is CANNOT DETERMINE (community says 90-95A). Resolve before release - 85A vs 95A changes the ground friction the sim assumes (condim 3, friction 1.0).
print_profiles.orientation: Sole tread face down, DEAD FLAT. WHY: the tread is the ground-contact surface and must be geometrically true - printed against the bed it takes the bed's own flatness. Ground reaction enters normal to it, so the layers see compression and interfacial shear, not tension, which is the only loading a 500 %-elongation elastomer laminate handles predictably.
print_profiles.supports: None (clean pad, no holes, 1.232 mm minimum wall). 40 % infill, not 100: a sole is a compliance element and its stiffness is a design variable, not something to maximise. NOTE the FEA cannot validate this - materials.json states that linear small-strain elasticity 'describes the first fraction of a percent' of TPU's useful range.

print_profiles.material: TPU (Bambu TPU 85A as sliced; durometer CANNOT DETERMINE).
print_profiles.orientation: Sole tread face down, dead flat - mirror, same reasoning.
print_profiles.supports: None.

print_profiles.material: TPU (Bambu TPU 85A as sliced; durometer CANNOT DETERMINE).
print_profiles.orientation: 8.4376 mm lip flat on the bed. WHY: a soft lip is loaded by contact pressure normal to its face; flat puts the layer stack in compression. It also gives an 87.6737 x 32.2339 contact patch, which matters because TPU and a no-brim policy do not mix well - this is the largest first layer available.
print_profiles.supports: None (no warning). Slow the first layer: TPU at 0.20 mm with no brim is adhesion-marginal, and the 44m39s quoted is already the second-longest print in the set.

print_profiles.material: TPU (Bambu TPU 85A as sliced; durometer CANNOT DETERMINE).
print_profiles.orientation: 3.2762 mm lip flat on the bed. WHY: same contact-pressure argument as jaw-soft, and at 3.2762 mm thick there is no other viable orientation - stood on edge it is an 87.8220 mm-long, 3.3 mm-thin wall in an elastomer.
print_profiles.supports: None. 16 layers total, so wall count and first-layer adhesion are the whole profile.

assumptions: FDM MACHINE-HOUR COST = $0.3198/h, built as: depreciation $1,249 / 5,000 print-hours = $0.2498/h (H2S launch price from 3dprint.com; the 5,000-hour divisor is 3dprintingcostcalculator.com's stated convention) + power $0.07/h (3dprintingcostcalculator.com's $0.06-0.08/h class figure for a Bambu-class machine). ASSUMPTION FLAG: the H2S has a 65 degC heated chamber whose draw is published nowhere we read, so the power term UNDERSTATES the H2S. CANNOT DETERMINE precisely; a plug-in meter on 192.168.1.133 settles it.

FILAMENT PRICES are layermath.com/filament-prices, 'Last data pass: Apr 2026': PLA $24.00/kg, PETG $29.00/kg, TPU $44.00/kg, ABS $27.00/kg. Bulk tiers applied to PLA only: $16.00/kg at qty 100 (Bambu's published 30 %-off-6+ tier, from a search snippet, NOT read off the store page - the store returned HTTP 402) and $10.00/kg at qty 1,000+ (Slant3D's stated membership price). NO BULK SOURCE EXISTS for PETG or TPU, so their price is held flat at every quantity - which makes the PETG and TPU unit costs CONSERVATIVE (too high) at volume.

WASTE AND FAILURE: material x 1.10 for purge/waste (3dprintingcostcalculator.com's stated multiplier); total x 1.10 for print failure (grandpacad's 10 % default; corroborated by pro.prusa3d.com's 90-95 % success rate).

LABOUR is $10.00 per robot = 2 plates x 15 min x $20/h, allocated to each piece pro-rata by its share of total print time. The $20/h rate and the 15-min-per-print hands-on figure are 3dprintingcostcalculator.com's. ASSUMPTION FLAG: this assumes plated printing (out/print/plates/ holds a 32-piece PLA plate and a 4-piece TPU plate). If the 36 pieces were handled individually it would be 36 x 15 min = 9 h = $180/robot, which would dwarf every other line. Support removal, reaming and heat-set insertion are NOT in this figure and are CANNOT DETERMINE.

PRINT TIME 12.346 h/robot is the SUM of per-piece seconds_total from out/print/slice.json. out/print/PRINT.md states 'a plate prints faster than its parts sum', so this is an UPPER BOUND; the actual plate time is not recorded anywhere and is CANNOT DETERMINE.

GRAMS AND SECONDS were sliced WITHOUT SUPPORTS on the 0.20mm Standard @BBL H2S preset. 11 of 30 parts carry slicer support warnings. All quoted grams and times are therefore LOWER BOUNDS. Switching 18 slugs to PETG, going to 100 % infill on the load path, and changing layer height on 8 parts each independently invalidate them. RE-SLICE before committing.

MOULDED PIECE PRICE = material + processing only (tooling is amortised separately in the break-even). Material = solid volume x 1.04 g/cm3 (ABS density, cecad/fits.py MATERIALS) x $2.00-4.50/kg (RapidDirect 2026 ABS resin range). Processing = cycle_s / 3600 x $40-80/h (zetarmold 2026 Asia machine rate) at ONE cavity. RUNNER AND SPRUE REGRIND ARE NOT INCLUDED - no source read gave a figure, so this UNDERSTATES the moulded cost, which biases the analysis TOWARD moulding and therefore strengthens the conclusion against it.

CYCLE TIME is DERIVED, not quoted: t_cool = 2.5 x s^2 seconds (s = wall in mm), calibrated on zetarmold's own two data points ('a 2mm wall part cooling for 10 seconds', 'A part with 4mm walls cooling for 40 seconds'); cycle = t_cool / 0.6 to t_cool / 0.8 (Jaycon 2026: 'Cooling represents 60 to 80% of the molding cycle'). Applied ONLY to the five parts with a measured nominal wall. For the other 25 the wall is CANNOT DETERMINE (docs/DFM.md reports thinnest wall, which is a knife-edge on most rows) and Jaycon 2026's real '25 to 35 second cycle' four-cavity reference is used instead. Sanity check: RJG's worked example (3.3 mm tensile bar, 18.00 s simulated / 16.73 s actual cooling) against the law's prediction of 27.2 s shows the law over-predicts by ~50 %, i.e. it is conservative.

TOOLING COST is MY BANDING of Jaycon 2026's sourced Class 105 aluminium range ($1,500-$8,000, 2-3 weeks): $1,500-3,000 for parts under 40 mm max dimension, $3,000-8,000 for 40-80 mm, $5,000-8,000 for over 80 mm or A-surface. The banding is my allocation, NOT a quote. Corroborating brackets read: RapidDirect Class 105 7075-T6 $2,000-5,000+ (500-10,000 shots); RJC $5,000 for a 1-cavity and $12,500 for a 4-cavity ABS consumer housing; zetarmold 'Simple prototype $2,000-6,000'; Protolabs 'Mold cost starts at $1,495' with a 2,000-shot guarantee. Protolabs also states a cam or insert adds GBP 1,000-2,000 PER COMPONENT - not added here, so the tooling figures are FLOORS for every part with a bearing bore or undercut, which is most of them.

BREAK-EVEN N* = T / (c_print - c_mould_piece_price), with c_print the IN-HOUSE FDM unit cost at the 10,000 tier and c_mould at its LEAST favourable (highest) sourced piece price. Where c_mould >= c_print the break-even is undefined and is reported as null, never as a large integer. A second break-even against a BOUGHT farm hour ($4/h, from layermath/prusa/grandpacad) is given in each rationale - it is 3-6x lower and is the number that applies if you do not own the machines.

MIRRORED PAIRS (shells L/R, upper legs, ankles, feet, soles) CANNOT SHARE A CAVITY. Identical pairs (yaw2roll x2, hip-bracket x2, shin x2, bearing-roll x2, neck-plate x2, rigidity-plate x2) can. Tooling counts assume one cavity set per slug; family moulds would cut the count and no source read tells us by how much - CANNOT DETERMINE.

MATERIAL SUBSTITUTION PLA -> PETG on the 18 load-path slugs is justified by materials.json's own tier rule ('a class figure may FAIL a check but may NOT PASS one'). PLA is class-tier with no grade and no spool; Bambu PETG Basic is grade-tier and confirmed:true against the Bambu Filament TDS V3.0. Cost of the switch: +$0.72 per robot. Mass: the load-path subset goes from 107.89 g as-sliced to 127.58 g at 100 % solid PETG, +19.7 g on a 737.2 g robot (+2.7 %).

100 % INFILL ON THE LOAD PATH is required for the FEA to describe the printed part - out/stress/report.json solves solids and the 0.20mm Standard preset does not print solids. If a lower infill is chosen, the FEA must be re-run at that density; there is no third option that leaves a PASS standing.

NO BRIM is a house rule taken from the brief, not from the repo. docs/DFM.md contradicts it at lines 78, 89, 109, 115 and 155; those notes must be struck. Sacrificial mouse-ear discs are specified in their place for the two upper legs, the only genuine adhesion risk once power-support and shin are laid flat.
EXCHANGE RATES were NOT fetched. Every figure is in the currency its source published. No EUR/GBP/USD conversion is performed anywhere in this analysis.

ASSEMBLY LABOUR, PACKAGING, CERTIFICATION, THE 15 XL330 SERVOS ($358.50, 75 % of read bought cost) AND ALL BOUGHT PARTS ARE OUT OF SCOPE HERE - they are in docs/PRODUCTION.md. This document prices only the make/print/mould decision on the 30 printed slugs, which is $21.86-23.73 per robot against a bought-parts floor of $472-481.

LICENCE: 22 of the 30 sliced STLs are Pollen vendor meshes under CC BY-SA-NC 4.0 - printable, simulable, renderable, NOT saleable. Every tooling decision in this document is conditional on either a licence from Pollen or a clean-room parametric rebuild. Only 8 slugs have a parametric rebuild today (banana-pcb-locker, bearing-roll, leg/shin, power-support, trunk-base, upper-leg L/R, yaw2roll, rigidity-plate per mech_dims.json rebuilt:true).

SLA WAS EVALUATED AND REJECTED, not omitted: no resin machine exists on the roster (five FDM machines only), and Protolabs Network states SLA parts are 'brittle... inclined to experience some creep' and 'generally not suitable for producing functional parts that can withstand... loads', with photopolymers becoming 'brittle and yellow under the influence of UV light' after 'a couple of months'. Both disqualifiers apply to this robot. Standard 405 nm resin at $17-30/L would have been cheap; the material behaviour, not the price, is what rules it out.
